conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… it’s this crampy pain in the middle of my stomach. It’s been going on for a while, but got worse a few days ago. I can’t keep anything down except a little soup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And have you had any fever, blood in your stool, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. I did feel a little feverish, but not sure. My stomach just hurts and I keep throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We checked your blood sugar when you came in, and it was high. You also had a small acid buildup, which we call a modest anion gap. That’s common in uncontrolled diabetes. We’re starting IV fluids and insulin to help correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know my sugars have been high. I’ve been stressed. I’ve been using my mom’s pain pills to help with the stomach pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you're allergic to morphine, so we won’t use that. But we’ll manage your pain safely. We also ordered a CT scan to check your abdomen. It showed some thickening in the colon, but it looks stable and not acute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? The colon thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been there a while, so it’s not an emergency. But we do need to check it further. The GI team recommends a sigmoidoscopy as an outpatient to make sure it’s not colitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I was supposed to get a stomach test before, but I never went.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a gastric emptying study. That’s still important. Given your diabetes and ongoing nausea, we think you might have gastroparesis — that’s when the stomach doesn’t empty properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel full and sick all the time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And it’s common in people with long-standing diabetes. We’ll need that test to confirm. We also want a stool test for H. pylori, since you had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I don’t want to stay in the hospital long. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re focused on getting your blood sugar under control and keeping you hydrated. The nausea is improving with anti-nausea meds. But you’ll need to follow up on those tests after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are better today. The acid in your blood has cleared, and your sugars are coming down with the insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I still feel kind of shaky though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching that. It could be from the insulin or from not eating. We’re trying to get you to tolerate small sips. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but not as bad. I’m just so anxious. I hate being in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatry team saw you yesterday. They think your anxiety is making things harder. They recommend starting mirtazapine at night for sleep and anxiety, and you can take Ativan up to three times a day as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on Celexa before. Did that help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They reviewed it and think it hasn’t been effective, so we’re stopping it. Mirtazapine might help more with both sleep and appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test came back. It showed mixed bacteria, but it’s likely contamination from skin or genital area, so we don’t think you have a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’re focusing on your diabetes, stomach issues, and anxiety. Your blood pressure is a bit high too, but we’ll manage that with your regular meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. You’ve been off IV fluids since this morning and tolerating small amounts of food. Your pain is less, and you’re not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to keep you a bit longer to finish monitoring, but we understand you want to leave. The GI team wanted to do the gastric emptying study and sigmoidoscopy here, but we can arrange them as outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather do them outside. I just can’t stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set that up. But it’s very important you schedule them soon. Gastroparesis and colon changes need to be checked properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I promise I’ll call. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your vitals are stable. You’ve been eating soft foods without vomiting. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue pantoprazole for stomach protection, ezetimibe for cholesterol, and your insulin. We’re adjusting your long-acting insulin to 8 units at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s lower than before. Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your sugars were high but now are improving. We don’t want you going too low, especially if you’re not eating well. You’ll also take half a mirtazapine pill at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Ativan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one tablet up to three times a day for anxiety. But don’t take more than that. We also recommend following up with a psychiatrist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I need help. I’ve been struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Case management is helping set up appointments at Central Clinic. It might be easier for you to go to one place for all your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would help. I get confused with all the different doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. Your discharge papers are ready. You’re stable, no fever, and you’ve been eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. What do I need to do next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, call your GI doctor to schedule the gastric emptying study and sigmoidoscopy. They’re important to understand your stomach and colon issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call today. I mean it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Also, take your new meds as directed. Watch your blood sugar closely. If you start vomiting again or your sugars go very high, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel really anxious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the Ativan as needed, but also try to reach your counselor. We’ve set up a case manager to help you stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll do better this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Take care, and please follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave — are you feeling okay to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m feeling much better. Still a little nervous, but I’ll be okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Remember, the Ativan is there if you need it. And call the clinic if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge instructions are in your packet. The key points are: schedule the GI tests, take your meds, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve already called the GI office. They’re mailing me the prep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Keep that momentum. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your insulin again before you leave. Make sure you’re comfortable with the doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I’ve got it. 8 units at night, and the fast-acting with meals based on my sugar and carbs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And use the sliding scale if your sugar is high. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your A1c was high at 9.7%. We know diabetes is hard to manage, especially with everything else going on. But controlling it helps prevent complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ll try harder. I don’t want to lose my kidneys or go blind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already taking steps. That’s what matters. We believe you can do this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay safe, and call if you need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you have a ride home and someone to check on you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my sister’s picking me up and staying tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take it easy, and we’ll talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take these printed instructions with you. Call the clinic Monday to confirm your appointments.
